newsitem.title: ITALY: SOCCER SHOWCASE-SAMP'S ETERNAL SON GLIMPSES PROMISED LAND.
newsitem.headline: SOCCER SHOWCASE-SAMP'S ETERNAL SON GLIMPSES PROMISED LAND.

text.p: Sampdoria's eternal son Roberto Mancini will get a rare glimpse of his promised land when he takes the field at Milan's Giuseppe Meazza stadium on Sunday.
Now the Genoa club's longest serving player, Mancini has twice dreamed of settling on the sacred turf of the San Siro.
First, in 1978, when only divine intervention in the form of the Italian postal service - the invite never arrived - denied the 13-year-old soccer wonder a tryout with AC Milan.
Then last November, when another 'higher authority' - in the form of club president Enrico Mantovani - vetoed Mancini's proposed move to Inter Milan.
In both cases, superstitious Sampdoria fans raised their eyes to the heavens and thanked the gods of soccer for granting them the most prolific scorer in Serie A.
"Without him, Sampdoria would be nothing," says Renzo Parodi, soccer correspondent for Genoa's "Il Secolo" newspaper. "He's our Eternal Father."
There is little doubt that when late president Paolo Mantovani bought Mancini in 1982, he saw him as the club's prodigal son.
"You can become for Sampdoria what Gianni Rivera was for Milan and Sandro Mazzola for Inter - a symbol," Mancini was told as he signed on the dotted line.
True to destiny, Sampdoria's emergence in the last decade as a rival to Milan, Juventus and Inter coincides with the rise and rise of the mercurial Mancini.
Samp's "number 10" scored in the club's first-ever major success, an Italian Cup victory over Milan in 1985.

The "terrible twins" partnership between Mancini and Gianluca Vialli not only scored the goals that brought the club their first league title in 1990/91, sometimes it even picked the teams and dictated the transfer campaign.
And even after Vialli's departure and Mantovani's death in 1993, captain Mancini became the guiding light for Samp's new generation team, currently lying second in the table.
Separated from his "twin", Vialli has often struggled to score goals but, time and again, Mancini's skill has given hitherto unheard of goalscorers prolific strike-rates.
Even in his prime, Ruud Gullit rarely scored more than a handful of goals at AC Milan; in his first season at Sampdoria, alongside Mancini, the Dutchman claimed a record haul of 15.
Last year, sharpshooter Enrico Chiesa struck 22 goals alongside Mancini. This season his replacement, Vincenzo Montella, has already found the net 12 times in 12 matches.
"Whenever he finds himself in front of goal, Roberto stops and looks for the best-placed team-mate," says Montella, searching for the secret to Mancini's reputation as "Assist Man."
But close observers of the Mancini phenomenon have noticed a new selfishness in his game. It has brought him 12 goals already this season, just three less than his personal best.
"By now, Mancini is capable of winning almost any match by himself," reported the daily Gazzetta dello Sport after he scored a hat-trick against Udinese.
"I've been working with Mancini for five years," admits his manager Sven-Goran Eriksson, "and I have to admit that the older he gets, the better he becomes."
Mancini likes to compare his ability to improve at the age of 32 to British sprinter Linford Christie, who won Olympic gold medal in his mid-thirties.
There are certainly parallels in their personalities.

Like Christie, the Mancini character is notoriously fragile off the pitch, with signs that the departure of close friends like Vialli and England's David Platt for richer pastures has widened his own horizons.
In an infamous incident last seaon, Mancini agonised over sacrificing his beloved Samp for a move to Arsenal to such an extent that he lost his cool on the pitch and was sent off.

Then, last November, there was another period of self-doubt with the proposed move to Inter - an incident which still suggests Mancini may take the field at the San Siro on Sunday for the last time in Sampdoria colours.
With hindsight, the death of Paolo Mantovani deprived Mancini of a father figure, a role that son Enrico cannot fill.
In his recently published autobiography, "I, Mancini", the player wrote a telling tribute to his founder-father: "To the man who always treated me like a fifth son."
Enticing offers are reportedly on the table from Blackburn - the likely destination of Eriksson next season - and Lazio.
Of couse, if Mancini has tired of his role as Samp's prodigal son, Italy's national team are looking for a prophet to lead them out of the post-Arrigo Sacchi wilderness.
National coach Cesare Maldini has said that the only serie A player capable of unpicking tight defences was Inter's Youri Djorkaeff -- playmaker for France!
"Maldini wants someone like Djorkaeff?" replied Mancini, "Mancini's a little bit like him."
